name: Aluminum chloride prescription (Drysol)

lead: Prescription aluminium chloride is for people whose sweat shows through clothes: it aims for dry underarms, hands or feet and far fewer sweat stains.

It is a stronger form of the ingredient in regular antiperspirants, blocking sweat ducts so less sweat reaches the skin. Guidelines list topical antiperspirants as first-line therapy for hyperhidrosis, and improvement is reported to take about three to five days.

paras: Prescribed by a clinician for hyperhidrosis and applied to dry skin on the affected area, typically as the step after over-the-counter antiperspirants stop being enough.
Skin irritation is the most common side effect. The FDA advises people with kidney dysfunction to consult a doctor first. It is prescription-only.

chain: Strong aluminium chloride blocks sweat ducts
angle.text: Prescription aluminium chloride is used for heavy sweating to stay dry and avoid visible sweat marks and odor. It blocks sweat ducts, and guidelines list topical antiperspirants as first-line hyperhidrosis therapy.

lead: Drysol is a brand of prescription topical aluminium chloride solution used for hyperhidrosis, or excessive sweating.[1] People use it for a presentation payoff: less visible sweat on underarms, hands, feet or face means fewer sweat stains on clothes, drier handshakes and a neater look through the day. Aluminium chloride is a stronger version of the ingredient in regular antiperspirants, and guidelines list topical antiperspirants as first-line therapy.[1]

Wikipedia reports that improvement takes about three to five days and that the most common side effect is skin irritation.[1] Case reports describe 20% aluminium chloride in alcohol (Drysol) used for localized sweating, including a woman with one-sided segmental hyperhidrosis and a patient with facial and scalp sweating treated with it alongside an oral medicine.[2][3] Hyperhidrosis is described in the dermatology literature as a psychosocially embarrassing condition.[4]

Training forums such as T Nation have threads in which lifters ask about heavy sweating and share what they use, including moisture-wicking clothing and, in one thread, a link to consumer information on prescription aluminium chloride.[5][6][7]
infobox: Aluminium chloride (20% in alcohol in case reports)[3]

paras: Hyperhidrosis may affect up to 2.8% of the US population, most often appearing between ages 25 and 64, with a family history in 30 to 50 percent of cases.[1] Higher-strength aluminium chloride antiperspirants have shown some success for hand and foot sweating.[1]

Beyond underarm sweating, Drysol has been reported for palmar and plantar sweating,[1] localized one-sided sweating,[3] and facial and scalp sweating in combination with oral clonidine in a single case report.[2] Dermatologists have also used aluminium chloride (Drysol) as a hemostatic agent in minor surgical procedures.[8]
Skin irritation is the most common side effect.[1] The FDA advises people with kidney dysfunction to consult a doctor before using aluminium antiperspirants.[9]

A 1978 case report described miliaria (heat rash) with exertion after repeated use of 20% aluminium chloride in a patient with segmental hyperhidrosis.[3] A 1993 report described an unusual histiocytic reaction in skin biopsies after topical aluminium chloride used as a hemostatic agent.[8]
Wikipedia cites Everdry as the first commercial antiperspirant in 1903.[9] Specific details about Drysol's development were not found in the sources loaded.

No controlled trials specific to Drysol appeared in the sources loaded. The published record consists of case reports,[2][3] a 1977 Medical Letter review titled 'Drysol for treatment of hyperhidrosis',[10] and the guideline summary in the Hyperhidrosis article, which cites an evidence-based review of nonsurgical management and guidance from the International Hyperhidrosis Society without giving trial results.[1] A case report on botulinum toxin for inguinal hyperhidrosis lists aluminium-salt antiperspirants such as Drysol among treatments of varied success.[4]

timeline.event: Everdry, the first commercial antiperspirant, marketed.[9]
